focus: Busan Political Crisis: open Army HQ Directive No.217 and triangulate martial-law/troop-transfer command chain

material_findings.finding: The primary text of Army Headquarters Directive No.217, 'To Army Soldiers', is now directly opened in the National Institute of Korean History's Materials on Korean History. It is dated 1952-05-27, addressed from Army Headquarters in Daegu to all unit commanders, and signed by Army Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Lee Jong-chan. The text states that the armed forces are not subordinate to any institution or individual, must remain aloof from political affairs, and must preserve the military chain of command.

Directive 217 itself does not name President Rhee, the martial-law commander, or a specific troop-transfer request. Therefore it is evidence of Lee Jong-chan's institutional neutrality position, but it must not by itself be represented as a written refusal addressed to Rhee.

A May 27 FRUS telegram by Chargé Lightner records Gen. Van Fleet stating that neither he nor the ROK Army Chief of Staff had been informed or consulted in advance of the martial-law decision. Van Fleet also said he had advised Gen. Lee that he would not approve transfers of combat troops to Pusan because this would weaken the front.

The same May 27 telegram preserves Rhee's own account that the cabinet decided on martial law, that he suggested including Pusan, and that because of urgency written orders from the Chief of Staff were not obtained. Rhee said he telephoned Gen. Lee, after which the defense minister would issue the decree, Won Yong-deok would be appointed martial-law commander, and Won would take orders directly from the President. This is a principal-actor account recorded contemporaneously by US diplomats and materially narrows the formal command-chain question, while still requiring the Korean decree/order for domestic primary confirmation.

Lightner further recorded that Rhee accused Lee Jong-chan of involvement in a plot and displayed messages he said Lee had sent to Won and other officers, allegedly countermanding the prior oral understanding and directing the martial-law commander not to act except under Lee's instructions. Van Fleet defended Lee's loyalty and described his commitment to keeping the army out of internal politics. The alleged Lee-to-Won messages are now a concrete primary-document target and must not be treated as verified until recovered.

A later November 3 FRUS memorandum records Gen. Lemnitzer's retrospective account that Rhee demanded two Korean divisions be moved south to execute martial law, Van Fleet refused the two-division request, and one company was nevertheless authorized and apparently moved to Pusan. This complicates any simple claim that Lee Jong-chan alone blocked troop movement: the UN command layer also exercised operational control and refusal authority over combat-unit transfer.

The command graph should therefore distinguish at least four layers: Rhee/cabinet political decision; Defense Ministry decree channel; Won Yong-deok's martial-law command; and ROK Army/UNC operational-control constraints on combat troop movement. Direct presidential control over Won, as reported by Rhee to Van Fleet and Lightner, must not be collapsed into proof that every arrest or detention order personally originated with Rhee.

The May 28 National Assembly record reproduced by NIHK shows the Assembly passed a resolution demanding termination of martial law in Pusan by 96-3 with 139 present, after debate explicitly referring to the forced detention of more than forty legislators' vehicle. This independently anchors legislative institutional opposition and the Assembly's own legal response rather than relying solely on US reporting.

The May 30 FRUS telegram records the US demand that martial law be lifted in Pusan and notes UNCURK's recommendation that detained Assembly members be released so the legislature could function normally. Rhee replied that martial law would be lifted shortly while defending the arrests as an internal matter. This supplies an adversarial pairing of external institutional criticism and Rhee's counter-position in one contemporaneous record.

June 2-4 FRUS records show the crisis was not solely Rhee versus foreign actors: on June 3 Prime Minister Chang reported that most cabinet members refused to support Rhee's proposed dissolution of the National Assembly, and Rhee backed down at least temporarily after cabinet resistance and Truman's intervention. This creates a cabinet-level opposed_by branch that should be separately modeled.

adversarial_checks: Directive 217 was opened in primary text and is no longer described from biography alone.
The directive is not mislabeled as a direct written refusal to Rhee because it names no such request.
Rhee's own May 27 explanation of the martial-law decision chain is preserved as a party account rather than discarded.
Van Fleet's operational-control role is separated from Lee Jong-chan's domestic chain-of-command position.
The later Lemnitzer account is marked retrospective and not silently treated as a same-day record.
Rhee's allegation that Lee countermanded instructions to Won is not treated as verified until the messages are recovered.
Direct presidential orders to Won are not generalized into proof of personal presidential authorship for each arrest.
The Assembly's May 28 legal response is checked against a domestic contemporaneous record, not only US diplomatic reporting.
UNCURK/US criticism and Rhee's counter-position are both preserved in the May 30 diplomatic record.
Cabinet resistance to dissolution is preserved, preventing the executive branch from being modeled as politically uniform.
US consideration of intervention is kept distinct from actions actually taken.
The one-company troop movement in Lemnitzer's account is retained as apparently moved, not upgraded to a fully documented Korean deployment order.
